summary:
Law 5089/2024 legalised same-sex marriage in Greece in February 2024, making the country the first with a majority Orthodox Christian population to do so. The same law added sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics (SOGIESC) as equal-treatment grounds across goods and services, education, healthcare, housing and social protection. Civil unions have been available since 2015, adoption and foster care by same-sex couples are permitted, and the age of consent is 15 for everyone.

Legal gender change has been available on a self-declaration basis since 2017. TGEU's Trans Rights Index and Map 2025 records Greece meeting 21 of its 32 indicators, with identified gaps including age restrictions on changes of forename, the absence of a national action plan on trans rights, and no legal recognition of trans or non-binary parenthood.

Conversion practices have been banned for minors and intersex genital mutilation criminalised since 2022. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity has been prohibited since 2023, and Greece's hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity. ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map placed Greece 7th in its 2025 ranking.

Violence against trans people remains documented. In March 2024 a mob of approximately 150 people attacked two transgender people in Thessaloniki; 21 people were arrested, 11 of them minors, and a masked attack on counter-protesters followed. In July 2025 the Crete Court of Appeal convicted three French tourists over a 2017 attack.

Police conduct toward visibly trans people has been the subject of an adverse judgment: in Koutra and Katzaki v. Greece (application 459/16, 2017) the European Court of Human Rights found that officers stopped and mistreated transgender sex workers and their lawyer in Athens in 2013, and that complaints against the officers were discontinued.

The same court condemned Greece in 2025 for detaining an LGBTI Iranian refugee pending deportation, finding a violation of Article 3. A criminal case has been opened over an online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people.

Self-reported experience in the EU Agency for Fundamental Rights LGBTIQ survey III (2024) shows constrained everyday conduct: 63% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner against an EU-27 figure of 53%, 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault against 29% EU-wide, and only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ against 51% across the EU.

Official and institutional hostility persists alongside the statutory framework. The Orthodox Church officially opposed marriage equality, and transphobic comments were directed at Greek Eurovision contestants in 2024.

The UK Foreign Office updated its travel advice for LGBTQ+ travellers to Greece in April 2024, noting that same-sex relations are legal, civil unions have existed since 2015, marriage has been available since February 2024, the age of consent is 15 for all, and legal gender change is possible, while advising travellers to remain alert.
tangentialFactors:
TGEU's 2025 index reports backsliding outpacing progress across Europe for the first time, so Greece's 21-of-32 score sits within a continental trend rather than an isolated national trajectory.

Greece's FRA survey results run several points above EU-27 averages on avoidance of public affection and of locations, and several points below on being open about being LGBTIQ, indicating a social climate less permissive than the statutory position suggests.

The Orthodox Church's formal opposition to marriage equality and the transphobic commentary around Eurovision are institutional and media signals of the reception a visibly trans visitor may encounter, independent of the legal position.

The legislative trajectory runs from a Justice Ministry working group on cohabiting same-sex couples pledged in 2008, through civil unions in 2015, to marriage equality in 2024; the pace of statutory change has outstripped documented change in street-level conditions.

Travel advice from the UK Foreign Office is an external risk signal rather than a legal instrument, and its April 2024 update coincided with the marriage-equality law rather than with any change in safety conditions.
localsOnly:
Placement of trans prisoners has been contested. In December 2021 the General Secretary for Crime-Prevention Policy, Sofia Nikolaou, ordered four trans detainees transferred to the women's prison of Korydallou after each had petitioned for transfer on the basis that they identify and wish to be treated as women. The four, three Greek and one Bulgarian, had been held at Trikala and Corfu prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender. The decision is recorded as the first documented transfer of trans prisoners to a women's facility in Greece; it also indicates that default placement had followed male facilities, with transfer to a women's facility available on request.

Discrimination in employment is reported at a higher rate than the EU average: 28% of LGBTIQ respondents to the FRA survey III (2024) felt discriminated at work, against 19% across the EU-27.

Greece has rules governing military service for LGBTI personnel; the specific terms of those rules are not set out in the sources available for this record.
outOfScopeNotes:
The content of the age restrictions on changes of forename identified as a gap by TGEU is not sourced here; the index records the gap but the underlying statutory provision is not quoted.

Whether the 2021 route for transferring trans prisoners to women's facilities has since been codified, extended to other facilities, or applied beyond the four named detainees is unresolved in the available sources.

The enforcement record for the 2023 employment-discrimination ban and for the hate-crime and hate-speech provisions covering gender identity is not documented in the inventory; no conviction data is available.

The outcome or current status of the criminal case opened over the online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people is unresolved.

Compliance with the 2025 European Court of Human Rights judgment on the detention of an LGBTI Iranian refugee, including any policy change on detention pending deportation, is not sourced.

Non-binary legal recognition is not addressed in any source; TGEU's reference to unrecognised trans and non-binary parenthood is the only indication, and no statutory position can be stated.
